Ass
AS
n. (rendering Hebrew chamōr and 'āthōn, Greek onos)
From Old English assa, ultimately from Latin asinus. The Hebrew chamōr is the male ass, probably from a root meaning reddish, the colour of the common Palestinian donkey; 'āthōn is the she-ass, the more valuable riding animal. The ass is an unclean beast under the law and yet is the mount of judges, of kings in peace, and at the last of the King Himself — a combination that carries the whole doctrine of lowliness the word is used to teach.

Biblical Definition

The ass is the beast of burden and of peace, and Scripture gives it a dignity the horse never receives. The horse in the Old Testament is the animal of war and of trust in armies; the ass is what a man rides when he comes in peace. That distinction governs the great messianic prophecy, where the King's arrival is announced with a deliberately humble mount: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Zec 9:9) — fulfilled to the letter on Palm Sunday, when the Lord Jesus deliberately chose the animal that declared what kind of king He was. The ass is also unclean, and so cannot be offered; the law therefore makes a startling provision, requiring that its firstborn be bought back by the death of a clean animal or else destroyed: “And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck: and all the firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem” (Exo 13:13). The unclean creature lives only because a lamb dies in its place, and the verse sets the redemption of a man's children in the same breath. Scripture also uses the ass to humble the prophet who thought he saw: “And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?” (Num 22:28) — the beast saw the angel the seer could not. And Proverbs puts it in a list of things governed by what they will answer to: “A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back” (Pro 26:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

A well-known beast of burden, patient and sure-footed, unclean under the law; in Scripture the mount of peace as the horse is of war, the beast redeemed by a lamb, the animal that rebuked Balaam, and the mount of the King entering Zion.

expand to see more

ASS, n. 1. A quadruped of the equine genus, having long slouching ears, a short mane, and a tail covered with long hairs at the end.

2. The ass is patient and sure-footed, and is used as a beast of burden, and in the east as a riding animal of dignity.

3. A dull, heavy, stupid fellow; a dolt; used in reproach.

4. Under the law an unclean beast, which might not be offered; its firstling was to be redeemed with a lamb, or its neck broken. Exod. 13.

5. In Scripture, thy King cometh unto thee... lowly, and riding upon an ass. Zech. 9.

Key Scripture

Zechariah 9:9 — "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass."

Exodus 13:13 — "And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck: and all the firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem."

Numbers 22:28 — "And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?"

Proverbs 26:3 — "A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back."

Modern Corruption

The talking ass of Numbers 22 is dismissed as folklore embedded in the text, and with it the whole class of miracle in which God overrules nature to rebuke a man who is professionally religious and spiritually blind.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on the word comes from the historical-critical treatment of Num 22 as a folk tale absorbed into the narrative — a charming survival rather than an event. The dictionary takes the account as history, and notes that the New Testament does the same: Peter refers to it as fact, saying the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet. The point of the episode is not the marvel but the reversal. The seer hired for his vision cannot see what his donkey sees, and is saved from the drawn sword of the angel by an animal he has beaten three times. God is perfectly able to make the beast wiser than the prophet, and He does it here to a man on his way to sell his gift for money.

The principle to recover concerns the mount of Zec 9:9. The prophecy specifies an ass rather than a horse, and the Lord Jesus arranged the detail deliberately, sending two disciples for the colt. The crowd that shouted Hosanna wanted a horse — a deliverer who would ride against Rome — and within the week the same city was crying crucify him, in part because He had come the way Zechariah said He would. He is still refused for the same reason. A king who arrives lowly, riding on a borrowed donkey, and whose throne is a cross, does not answer to the expectations men bring to religion; and the temptation to prefer a Christ on a war horse is not confined to the first century.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chamōr is the male ass, and 'āthōn the she-ass; 'ayir is the young ass or colt, the word in Zec 9:9. Greek onos is an ass, and pōlon onou the colt of an ass.

expand to see more

Hebrew chamōr (H2543) — a male ass, probably from a root meaning reddish; the common beast of burden.

Hebrew 'āthōn (H860) — a she-ass, the more valuable riding beast; the animal Balaam rode (Num 22:28).

Hebrew 'ayir (H5895) — a young ass or colt; a colt the foal of an ass (Zec 9:9), never yet broken to a rider.

Hebrew pe'er / peter (H6363) — that which openeth the womb, the firstling; the firstling of an ass must be redeemed with a lamb (Exo 13:13).

Greek onos (G3688) — an ass; and hupozugion (G5268), a beast under the yoke, the word Matthew uses in quoting Zechariah.

Usage

"Of the King's lowly entry: thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass (Zec 9:9)."

"Of the unclean redeemed by a lamb: every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb (Exo 13:13)."

"Of the beast that saw what the prophet could not: the LORD opened the mouth of the ass (Num 22:28)."
